questions.explain: The DBA's signature for parameter sniffing: one query shows wildly varying runtimes while using the same plan hash — the plan was optimized for the first execution's parameter values. Mitigations include OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR hints, and Query Store forced plans.
options: One query with a different plan hash on every execution.
One query with wildly varying runtimes but the same plan hash — the cached plan was shaped by the first execution's parameter values.
A query whose text changes between executions.
A query that only runs slowly when the connection pool is exhausted.
questions.q: A DBA suspects parameter sniffing on a SQL Server API query. What signature should they look for?

questions.explain: Serialization failures (error 3960) and deadlocks (error 1205) are recoverable — retry with exponential backoff. Pool exhaustion should fail fast with 503 + Retry-After rather than queuing indefinitely.
options: Treat all database errors as fatal and return a 500 to the client.
Retry serialization failures (error 3960) and deadlocks (error 1205) with backoff; respond to pool exhaustion with a fast 503 + Retry-After instead of queueing indefinitely.
Always queue requests indefinitely when the pool is exhausted so none are lost.
Retry only deadlock errors; serialization failures must always be reported as bugs.
questions.q: How should API code respond to the three error categories the chapter distinguishes — serialization failures (3960), deadlocks (1205), and connection pool exhaustion?

questions.explain: OFFSET N forces the database to scan and discard the first N rows; deep pages get expensive. Keyset pagination anchors on the last-seen key value (e.g., created_at + order_id) and uses an index seek at any depth — but it can only walk forward sequentially, not jump to an arbitrary page.
options: Keyset pagination can jump to any page number; offset pagination cannot.
Keyset pagination requires full table scans on every request.
Offset-based pagination scans and discards N rows for OFFSET N, degrading at depth; keyset pagination uses an index seek at any depth but can only walk forward sequentially.
Both approaches have identical performance; the choice is purely stylistic.
questions.q: What is the performance tradeoff between offset-based (OFFSET-FETCH) and keyset (cursor-based) pagination?

questions.explain: A transaction should encompass exactly the database operations that must succeed or fail together. Transactions held open across external network calls hold locks and block version-store cleanup under RCSI/snapshot, bloating tempdb; conversely, related writes executed without any transaction risk partial failure.
options: Transactions should stay open for the full HTTP request lifetime so everything is atomic.
A transaction should cover exactly the database work that must succeed or fail together — no external network calls inside it, and no multi-step operations left un-transactioned.
Short transactions are always wrong; use one long transaction per API endpoint.
Savepoints eliminate the need to ever think about transaction scope.
questions.q: What is the correct design principle for transaction scope in API handlers, and what goes wrong at each extreme?

questions.explain: Carrying a correlation ID (Application Name keyword, sp_set_session_context) into the session lets the DBA attribute expensive queries to a specific HTTP request/endpoint — the difference between a five-minute diagnosis and a two-hour investigation.
options: It propagates a correlation ID from the HTTP request into the database session, letting the DBA attribute queries to the exact API endpoint during an incident.
It reduces the number of connections the pool needs.
It enables automatic retry of failed transactions.
It encrypts the traffic between the API and the database.
questions.q: Why is propagating a correlation ID from the HTTP request into the database session so valuable to a DBA?
